approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (2017 Measures No. 5) Bill 2017
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that would create a new licensing system for administrators of important financial benchmarks, overseen by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission would gain authority to designate significant benchmarks and make rules based on international principles, and manipulating a financial benchmark would become a criminal offence.
The main parts of the bill would start the day after the bill receives royal assent.
Create a new licensing regime for administrators of designated significant financial benchmarks.
Give ASIC powers to make rules for licensed benchmark administrators.
Make manipulation of financial benchmarks a criminal offence with civil penalties.
Administrators of designated significant financial benchmarks and entities from which ASIC may recover regulatory costs.

Labor supported the bills strengthening financial benchmark manipulation laws and ASIC cost recovery, but announced it will move a Senate amendment to replace the bill's race-based definition of "Indigenous person" with the modern three-part Commonwealth working definition of descent, identification and community acceptance.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (2017 Measures No. 5) Bill 2017 and the ASIC Supervisory Cost Recovery Levy Amendment Bill 2017 introduce a new regulatory regime for financial benchmarks, including licensing, criminal and civil penalties (up to 10 years imprisonment and fines of nearly $10 million), and cost recovery levies, while also expanding the Productivity Commission to include a new Indigenous policy commissioner. The government argued that the existing legislative definition of an 'Indigenous person' should be retained.

The speaker supported not blocking the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill but argued that the government's approach to defining indigeneity and the appointment of an Indigenous policy commissioner to the Productivity Commission are inseparable from the bill's regulatory measures.

Labor argued the bill strengthens penalties and licensing for financial benchmark manipulation, citing ASIC cases against the big four banks over bank bill swap rate manipulation. The speaker also criticised the government for cutting ASIC's funding by $120 million in 2014 and resisting a royal commission into banking for 600 days, while noting Labor’s past reforms on consumer credit and financial advice.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (2017 Measures No. 5) Bill 2017 and related bill strengthen protections against manipulation of financial benchmarks and create a productivity commissioner with Indigenous experience; Labor supports the bills but criticises the government’s cuts to ASIC, its opposition to a banking royal commission, and the bill’s use of a race‑based definition of “Indigenous person” rather than the standard three‑part test.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill and ASIC Supervisory Cost Recovery Levy Amendment Bill, arguing for stronger criminal penalties for financial benchmark manipulation—including fines up to $9.45 million for corporations—and a new licensing regime for benchmark administrators. He also criticised the government’s $120 million cut to ASIC in 2014, called for a genuine banking royal commission, and raised concerns about the definition of Indigeneity in the Productivity Commission reform, urging the Prime Minister to support the Uluru Statement from the Heart.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill, which introduces a regulatory regime for financial benchmark administrators and adds a Productivity Commissioner for Indigenous policy. They also praised the Northern Territory government's $1.30 floor price on alcohol to address problem drinking and advocated for a federal volumetric alcohol tax, while criticising the Prime Minister's opposition to an Indigenous voice to parliament.

Labor supports the bill but objects to schedule 2, which would replace the established three-part administrative definition of Aboriginality (descent, self-identification, community acceptance) with a race-based definition for the new Productivity Commissioner role.

The speaker argued that the bill should replace an outdated race-based definition of Indigeneity with a modern three-part definition (descent, self-identification, community recognition), and noted that the government eventually agreed to omit the old definition. The speaker also thanked staff member Nick Green for his work on the amendment.
